question: A ten-person startup is moving its containerized web application from a single VM to Kubernetes. The team has no dedicated platform engineers, wants Google to manage node provisioning, security hardening and upgrades, and prefers to pay only for the resources its Pods request. Which GKE option should you recommend?
options: A GKE Standard cluster with node auto-provisioning enabled and node auto-upgrade turned on.
A GKE Autopilot cluster, which manages nodes, enforces hardened defaults and bills per Pod resource request.
A GKE Standard cluster with a single node pool of Spot VMs to minimize cost.
A GKE Enterprise fleet with Config Sync so that cluster configuration is managed from Git.
explanation: Autopilot is the Google-recommended mode for teams that want a fully managed Kubernetes experience: Google provisions and scales nodes, applies security best practices (for example Workload Identity and Shielded nodes by default), handles upgrades, and charges for Pod CPU, memory and storage requests rather than for whole nodes. Option A still leaves node pool operations, sizing and security configuration to the team and bills per node. Option C reduces cost but Spot nodes can be preempted and the team must still operate nodes. Option D addresses configuration management across many clusters and does not remove node management responsibilities.
hint: Core Rule (GKE Autopilot vs Standard): Autopilot is the Google-recommended mode for teams that want a fully managed Kubernetes experience: Google provisions and scales nodes, applies security best practices (for example Workload Identity and Shielded nodes by default), handles upgrades, and charges for Pod CPU, memory and storage requests rather than for whole nodes.

question: A medical imaging company runs a GKE Standard cluster that hosts both a REST API and a set of image-classification workers that need NVIDIA L4 GPUs. The GPU nodes are expensive and the company has noticed that ordinary API Pods are being scheduled on them, wasting GPU capacity. What should you do?
options: Enable node auto-provisioning so that GKE decides where every Pod should run.
Increase the CPU requests of the API Pods so that they no longer fit on the GPU nodes.
Move the GPU workers to a separate GKE Autopilot cluster so that GPU nodes are never shared.
Create a dedicated GPU node pool with a node taint, add a matching toleration and node selector to the classification workers, and keep the API Pods on the general-purpose node pool.
explanation: Node pools are the mechanism for grouping nodes with specific hardware, and a taint on the GPU pool prevents Pods without a matching toleration from landing there; GKE automatically adds the nvidia.com/gpu taint to GPU node pools for this reason, and a node selector or affinity on the workers ensures they land on the GPU pool. Option A does not stop general Pods from being placed on GPU nodes. Option B is a fragile side effect rather than a scheduling policy and may not work as the pool scales. Option C introduces a second cluster and cross-cluster networking just to solve a scheduling problem that taints solve natively.
hint: Core Rule (GKE node pools): Node pools are the mechanism for grouping nodes with specific hardware, and a taint on the GPU pool prevents Pods without a matching toleration from landing there; GKE automatically adds the nvidia.com/gpu taint to GPU node pools for this reason, and a node selector or affinity on the workers ensures they land on the GPU pool.

question: A data-science platform on GKE Standard runs hundreds of short-lived jobs whose resource requests vary widely: some need 2 vCPUs, others need 64 vCPUs and 400 GB of memory, and a few need GPUs. What should you do?

Option C is not viable for jobs that need hundreds of gigabytes of memory or GPUs beyond Cloud Run limits and ignores the existing Kubernetes investment. Option D changes what Pods request, not whether suitable nodes exist.
hint: Core Rule: Node auto-provisioning (NAP) extends the cluster autoscaler so that GKE automatically creates node pools with machine types, GPUs and sizes that match pending Pods' requirements and deletes them when unused, which removes the manual node pool management described.

question: A global bank operates 30 GKE clusters across several regions and two on-premises data centers. Each cluster must have identical namespaces, RBAC roles, network policies and resource quotas, and auditors must be able to trace every configuration change to a reviewed commit. Today changes are applied by hand and clusters drift. What should you do?
options: Write a Cloud Build pipeline that runs kubectl apply against every cluster whenever the repository changes.
Use Terraform's Kubernetes provider to define the resources and run terraform apply nightly against each cluster.
Register all clusters to a GKE Enterprise fleet and enable Config Sync so that each cluster continuously reconciles the shared configuration from a Git repository.
Create a golden cluster, export its configuration with kubectl get -o yaml, and re-import it into the other clusters every month.
explanation: Config Sync, enabled at fleet level, installs an in-cluster agent on every registered GKE or attached cluster that pulls the desired state from Git and continuously reconciles it, so drift is corrected automatically and every change is a reviewed commit; fleets also let you apply the same configuration to on-premises clusters. Option A pushes configuration but does not detect or revert drift between runs and needs credentials to every cluster. Option B has the same push-model limitation and a nightly window in which drift persists. Option D is manual, error-prone and provides no audit trail.
hint: Core Rule (GKE Enterprise fleets and Config Sync): Config Sync, enabled at fleet level, installs an in-cluster agent on every registered GKE or attached cluster that pulls the desired state from Git and continuously reconciles it, so drift is corrected automatically and every change is a reviewed commit; fleets also let you apply the same configuration to on-premises clusters.

question: A healthcare SaaS provider must ensure that no workload on its GKE Enterprise clusters runs as a privileged container, uses the latest image tag, or lacks resource limits. Violations must be rejected at admission time, and the security team wants a dashboard of existing violations across all clusters. What should you do?

question: A video-streaming service runs the same set of microservices in GKE clusters in us-central1, europe-west1 and asia-southeast1. The company wants a single anycast IP address and hostname for its public API, requests routed to the nearest healthy cluster, automatic failover if a cluster's backends become unhealthy, and the ability for application teams to manage their own HTTP routes using standard Kubernetes APIs. What should you do?

Option B provides regional routing by DNS only, which is slow to fail over because of resolver caching and offers no health-based global load balancing. Option C uses self-managed components and an external product where a native solution exists. Option D adds an unnecessary hop and does not integrate with Kubernetes routing APIs.
hint: Core Rule: Multi-cluster Gateway builds on the Kubernetes Gateway API and the global external Application Load Balancer: a single Gateway in the config cluster programs one anycast IP whose backends are Pods in all fleet member clusters, so traffic goes to the closest healthy cluster with automatic failover, while HTTPRoutes allow teams to own their routing in a standard API.

question: An e-commerce company's GKE workloads authenticate to Cloud Storage and Pub/Sub using a service account JSON key that is mounted as a Kubernetes Secret. A security review flagged the long-lived key as a risk. You need to remove the key while allowing each Kubernetes service account to receive only the permissions it needs, following Google-recommended practices. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

Rotate the JSON key every 30 days with a Cloud Scheduler job and store it in Secret Manager instead of a Kubernetes Secret.

Grant the required IAM roles to each Kubernetes service account principal (or bind it to a dedicated IAM service account) so that each workload gets only the permissions it needs.
Use the Kubernetes Secrets Store CSI driver to fetch the JSON key from Secret Manager at Pod start time.
explanation: Workload Identity Federation for GKE lets Pods authenticate as their Kubernetes service account and receive short-lived Google credentials without any exported key, and binding IAM roles per Kubernetes service account gives least-privilege access for each workload. Option B keeps a long-lived key in circulation; rotating and moving it does not eliminate the risk. Option C removes the key but gives every Pod on the node the same broad identity, violating least privilege. Option E still relies on an exported key, just delivered differently.
hint: Core Rule (Workload Identity for GKE): Workload Identity Federation for GKE lets Pods authenticate as their Kubernetes service account and receive short-lived Google credentials without any exported key, and binding IAM roles per Kubernetes service account gives least-privilege access for each workload.

question: A logistics company runs a revenue-critical order-management system on GKE Standard. The operations team wants Google to keep the control plane and nodes automatically patched, but it wants new Kubernetes minor versions to have been proven in the field for as long as possible before they reach production. Option A exposes production to the newest, least-proven releases. Option B removes automatic patching and leaves the cluster unsupported between manual upgrades. Option C is wrong because the Extended channel is intended to prolong support of an older minor version, not to provide the most-proven current versions, and Rapid pre-production would test versions two channels ahead.
hint: Core Rule (GKE release channels): Release channels provide automatic, Google-managed upgrades with different levels of maturity: Rapid gets versions first, Regular follows after they have been qualified, and Stable receives them last after additional soak time, so Stable for production and Regular for pre-production gives the requested early testing and maximum maturity.

question: A subscription-box company has a containerized Python script that reconciles the previous day's orders against payment records. question: A document-conversion API on Cloud Run renders PDFs with a single-threaded library that allocates up to 1.5 GB of memory per request. The service is configured with 2 GB of memory and the default concurrency of 80. Under load, instances crash with out-of-memory errors and p99 latency is very high, even though Cloud Run reports low instance counts. What should you do?

Set minimum instances to 20 so that enough instances are always warm to absorb the load.

Option C affects CPU allocation outside request handling and is irrelevant to this bottleneck.

question: A security operations team wants a Cloud Run service to be invoked whenever anyone creates a new firewall rule in any project of the organization, so that the rule can be reviewed and, if necessary, disabled within seconds. The team does not want to modify how firewall rules are created and wants a fully managed event path. What should you do?

Option B is polling with per-minute latency and heavy API usage. Option C detects certain misconfigurations but is not a general, near-real-time hook on rule creation and only notifies. Option D depends on every team's cooperation and cannot cover rules created outside Terraform.

question: A ride-sharing company must send a receipt through a third-party email API after each completed trip. The email API enforces a limit of 50 requests per second and occasionally returns errors that should be retried with exponential backoff. Trips peak at 2,000 completions per second. The receipts must be sent eventually but do not need to be immediate, and the team wants to avoid writing rate-limiting logic. Which service should you use to dispatch the email calls?
options: Publish each trip to a Pub/Sub topic with a push subscription targeting a Cloud Run service that calls the email API.
Write each trip to Firestore and have a Cloud Scheduler job invoke a Cloud Run function every second to send up to 50 emails.
Use Eventarc to route trip-completed events directly to a Cloud Run service with maximum instances set to 1.

Create a Cloud Tasks queue with a maximum dispatch rate of 50 per second and a retry configuration with exponential backoff, and enqueue an HTTP task per trip that targets a Cloud Run service which calls the email API.
explanation: Cloud Tasks is purpose-built for controlled, asynchronous execution: queues support explicit rate limits (dispatches per second, maximum concurrent dispatches) and per-queue retry policies with exponential backoff, so the third-party limit is respected without custom code and bursts are absorbed in the queue. Option A delivers as fast as possible and Pub/Sub push has no per-second rate limit control, so the email API would be overwhelmed. Option B is a hand-built scheduler with one-second granularity and custom bookkeeping. Option C uses max instances as a crude throttle, which does not guarantee 50 requests per second and causes Eventarc retries and back-pressure problems.
hint: Core Rule: Cloud Tasks is purpose-built for controlled, asynchronous execution: queues support explicit rate limits (dispatches per second, maximum concurrent dispatches) and per-queue retry policies with exponential backoff, so the third-party limit is respected without custom code and bursts are absorbed in the queue.

question: A regional bank needs to run an end-of-day process every evening: call an internal Cloud Run service to close the ledger, wait for a BigQuery job to finish, call a partner's REST API, and finally send a Pub/Sub message. options: Deploy Cloud Composer and write an Airflow DAG that chains the steps and is scheduled nightly.
Define the sequence in Workflows with built-in connectors and retry policies, and trigger the workflow with a Cloud Scheduler job every evening.
Write a single Cloud Run function that performs all four steps in order and schedule it with Cloud Scheduler.
Create four Cloud Scheduler jobs spaced 15 minutes apart, one per step, so that each step runs after the previous one should have finished.
explanation: Workflows is a serverless orchestrator for sequencing HTTP-based services and Google Cloud APIs: it passes outputs between steps, has connectors for BigQuery and Pub/Sub that handle long-running operations, and supports declarative retry and error handling, and Cloud Scheduler is the standard way to start it on a schedule. Option A meets the requirements but requires operating a Composer environment, which the team explicitly wants to avoid and which is aimed at data pipelines rather than simple service orchestration. Option C hides the orchestration in code, hits function timeout limits while waiting for BigQuery, and complicates retries. Option D relies on timing assumptions and breaks whenever a step runs long or fails.
hint: Core Rule (Workflows and Cloud Scheduler): Workflows is a serverless orchestrator for sequencing HTTP-based services and Google Cloud APIs: it passes outputs between steps, has connectors for BigQuery and Pub/Sub that handle long-running operations, and supports declarative retry and error handling, and Cloud Scheduler is the standard way to start it on a schedule.

question: A mobile gaming company runs a matchmaking API on Cloud Run written in Java with Spring Boot. Players complain that the first request after periods of low traffic, and requests during sudden scale-out, take 4 to 8 seconds. The company accepts a modest increase in cost but needs cold-start latency reduced significantly with configuration changes rather than a rewrite. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)
options: Configure a minimum number of instances so that warm instances are always available to serve the first requests.
Enable startup CPU boost so that the container gets additional CPU during initialization and the JVM starts faster.
Set the maximum number of instances to 1 so that no new instances need to start.
Migrate the service to a Cloud Run job so that the JVM stays resident between executions.
Increase the request timeout to 300 seconds so that slow first requests do not fail.
explanation: Two configuration-only levers directly attack cold-start latency: minimum instances eliminate cold starts after idle periods by keeping warm instances (at a reduced idle price), and startup CPU boost temporarily grants extra CPU while the instance starts, which materially shortens JVM startup during scale-out. Option C would cap capacity at one instance and create massive queuing under load. Option D is wrong because jobs are for run-to-completion tasks and cannot serve API requests. Option E only avoids timeout errors; it does not make the requests faster.
hint: Core Rule (Cloud Run cold-start optimization): Two configuration-only levers directly attack cold-start latency: minimum instances eliminate cold starts after idle periods by keeping warm instances (at a reduced idle price), and startup CPU boost temporarily grants extra CPU while the instance starts, which materially shortens JVM startup during scale-out.

question: A media company has an existing App Engine standard application written in Python. A new feature requires a native library that is not available in the standard runtime, needs to open long-lived WebSocket connections, and must write temporary files larger than the standard environment's in-memory file system allows. The team wants to keep using App Engine and its deployment tooling. What should you do?
options: Keep the application in App Engine standard and move the native library call into a Cloud Run function that the application invokes.
Rewrite the application to run on GKE Autopilot so that any library can be installed.
Deploy the new component as a separate App Engine flexible environment service using a custom runtime container, and route requests to it with a dispatch.yaml file.
Upgrade the App Engine standard application to the latest Python runtime, which supports arbitrary native libraries and WebSockets.
explanation: The App Engine flexible environment runs Docker containers on Compute Engine VMs, so it supports custom runtimes with native dependencies, WebSockets and local disk, and an application can mix standard and flexible services with dispatch rules, which keeps the existing tooling and codebase intact. Option A moves one library call but does not solve WebSockets or the temporary file requirement. Option B is a much larger migration than necessary and abandons the App Engine tooling the team wants to keep. Option D is incorrect because App Engine standard still sandboxes the runtime, does not support WebSockets, and provides only an in-memory /tmp file system.
hint: Core Rule (App Engine flexible vs standard): The App Engine flexible environment runs Docker containers on Compute Engine VMs, so it supports custom runtimes with native dependencies, WebSockets and local disk, and an application can mix standard and flexible services with dispatch rules, which keeps the existing tooling and codebase intact.

question: A bioinformatics company runs a GKE Standard cluster that hosts a latency-sensitive API and a large number of fault-tolerant genome-alignment batch Pods. Compute costs are dominated by the batch workload. The company wants to reduce cost significantly without risking the API's availability when Google reclaims capacity. What should you do?
options: Convert the entire cluster's node pools to Spot VMs and add PodDisruptionBudgets to the API deployment.
Purchase committed use discounts for the whole cluster and keep all node pools on standard VMs.
Run the batch Pods on a Cloud Run service with minimum instances set to zero so they cost nothing between runs.

Add a Spot VM node pool for the batch workload, rely on the automatic Spot taint so only Pods with the matching toleration and node selector are scheduled there, and keep the API on the standard node pool.
explanation: Mixing node pools lets you match volatility to workload tolerance: GKE automatically taints Spot nodes with cloud.google.com/gke-spot, so only the batch Pods that tolerate it land on the cheap, preemptible capacity, while the API stays on standard nodes and is unaffected by reclamation (cost optimization without sacrificing reliability). Option A puts the API on Spot capacity, and a PodDisruptionBudget cannot prevent a preemption. Option B saves less than Spot for the batch work and keeps the API cost unchanged. Option C is a different platform, and Cloud Run services are request-driven, not suited to long batch computations.
hint: Core Rule (GKE Spot node pools): Mixing node pools lets you match volatility to workload tolerance: GKE automatically taints Spot nodes with cloud.google.com/gke-spot, so only the batch Pods that tolerate it land on the cheap, preemptible capacity, while the API stays on standard nodes and is unaffected by reclamation (cost optimization without sacrificing reliability).

question: A media analytics company created a GKE private cluster in which nodes have no external IP addresses. question: A software company operates several GKE Standard clusters. Move all workloads to a single very large cluster to reduce the number of upgrades to perform.
Set the control plane to a static version and upgrade node pools manually with surge upgrades.

question: A legal-tech firm must re-index 50,000 PDF documents stored in Cloud Storage after every schema change. Indexing one document takes about 3 seconds and is independent of all others. The firm wants the whole run to complete in minutes rather than hours, wants failed documents retried automatically, and wants to avoid provisioning any cluster or VMs. What should you do?
options: Deploy the indexer as a Cloud Run service and have a Cloud Run function loop through the object list and call the service synchronously for each document.
Create a Dataproc cluster and run a Spark job that partitions the object list across executors.

Create a Cloud Run job with a task count of, for example, 200 and a parallelism of 200, have each task use the CLOUD_RUN_TASK_INDEX and CLOUD_RUN_TASK_COUNT environment variables to select its shard of the object list, and set a per-task retry limit.

explanation: Cloud Run jobs natively support array-style parallel execution: you specify how many tasks make up an execution and how many run concurrently, each task learns its index and the total count from injected environment variables so it can process a deterministic slice of the work, and failed tasks are retried up to the configured maximum, all without clusters or VMs. Option A serializes the work through one caller and risks the caller's own timeout. Option B provisions a cluster the firm wants to avoid and is heavyweight for independent tasks. Option D requires a Kubernetes cluster and a 50,000-completion Job is far less efficient than sharding.
hint: Core Rule (Cloud Run jobs parallelism): Cloud Run jobs natively support array-style parallel execution: you specify how many tasks make up an execution and how many run concurrently, each task learns its index and the total count from injected environment variables so it can process a deterministic slice of the work, and failed tasks are retried up to the configured maximum, all without clusters or VMs.
